Research life / Personal reflections

My PhD Experience

By Rohit Shrivastava · 8 min read

The journey of Ph.D is like a roller coaster ride, it will have ups and downs, both personally and professionally. Sometimes more downs and if you are wise and lucky then more ups. But, overall, its a learning experience. A successful Ph.D is more about keeping yourself motivated and manging people around you while doing some meaningful research.

I secured a Ph.D position after lot of failed attempts. I realised I was so rigid in chosing a topic for PhD that I even wrote 2 grants to do Ph.D on topics that I wished to work on. Now, I know, that it was not required from me. Anyways, thanks to the 2 PIs who helped me and guided me during grant writing. It certainly improved my writing skills. During my hunt to secure a funded Ph.D, I also figured out the missing skills from my CV that were bottleneck to getting a desired Ph.D. I also realised that the world is unfair place with some people having more chances of getting a Ph.D. However, during this period I worked in various lab and significantly improved my scientific skills.

After countless applications, few research proposals, numerous improvements in CV, suggestions from friends, a written exam, presentation and 3 interviews. I secured a desired Ph.D position in Israel. But I didn’t had any clue how life will be in this country. Although, I lived and worked in UK before coming to Israel, but I had a culture shock upon landing in Israel.

Anyways, first few weeks were spent mostly in reviewing the literature, discussions with my PI, reading the grant application and formulating my research goals. I was eager to do benchwork so I started working after 2 weeks of reading. Call it beginners luck or just co-incidence, initially experiments worked perfectly and my PI was happy with my progress, she even predicted I will have wonderful publications. Anyhow, I was enjoying the new found social life in Israel with occasional walk-ins to salsa lessons and trips to various historical sites in Israel as well as some course works. However, eventually things stopped working and I had no idea why. Since, the Post-doc in our lab had left by then and nobody had the hands on experience with experiments I was doing, I had to figure out problem myself. In order to optimize, I worked day and night to make experiments work, but nothing worked. I was doing experiments but data generated was meaningless, it was then I felt lowest of the low. I lost my motivation and enthusiasm. I realised how closely my self-worth was associated with my work.

After struggling for over 6 months, I decided to move on to some other experiments. It was then I got the opportunity to learn confocal microscopy. After initial hiccups, I was doing something which was giving me results. After a long time, I heard appreciation from my supervisor and I felt like I’m the star of the lab.

Gradually 1 year was over and I had to submit a research proposal for my Ph.D. In the time between submission and “Ph.D Proposal Defense” I was still looking for solution for my experiment, I also spoke to few Professors at conferences. Eventually, I decided to throw old cells and thaw out new cells and decided to clandestinely do the experiment again. I was hoping to troubleshoot but not hoping for the results in first try. To my surprise, the experiment worked. I called my supervisor to tell the good news but before hearing me she got annoyed that I’m wasting time. But I repeated again, she eventually paid attention to my words and was happy that the experiment worked. So for the Ph.D proposal exam, I had much more results to show than what I submitted in the research proposal. All the examiners were happy with my results and everything was going on smoothly. In fact, I managed to successfully do experiments about which examiners were skeptical. I then went to Translation UK conference and got positive comments on my poster. So all going well and I was feeling like I conquered the world.

​During this time, another surprise was waiting for me – my supervisor reduced my fellowship citing mismanagement of the funds. I was infuriated but couldn’t do anything but to swallow the bitter truth and move on. I returned back to work, at that time I was working 7 days a week. I had no social life.

​By now I have reached third year of my Ph.D so it was time to start summarising my results for the manuscript. I took 3 months to write the first draft and then after 6 months of editing and reviewing by my supervisor, manuscript was out. The first journal sent it back saying its not in their scope and that there is little new information. It was disappointing but we decided to submit to a parasitology specific journal. Finally, they took it and sent it for review. After 1 month came the reviewers comments and it was like a meltdown of global proportion – they rejected the manuscript and suggested to repeat 90% of the experiments again. I felt like someone had thrown me into hell and frying me in pan of oil. That day I didn’t slept well, kept thinking about the comments. Next day, I spoke with my supervisor that we can combine the new results with the results from the rejected manuscript and send it else where. However, instead of thinking over what I was saying she said I’m in depression so will discuss after a week. I don’t know if I was in depression but I was certainly annoyed that my so much time was wasted and have to do everything again. I was asking myself – “What is the point of having a Ph.D supervisor when the reviewers have to tell me that the way experiments were done is not right”. I didn’t wanted to speak to my supervisor and I avoided even looking at her. In fit of rage, I said that I’m learning more from the reviewers comments than from my supervisor. But, after a two or three weeks, I realised that I have to fix this mess and the easiest way is to do what reviewers have asked me to do. However, reviewers tell you what they want to see but not how to do it. We took help of a bio-informatics student, of whom my Prof was co-supervisor. He suggested us ways to do one of the experiment but it didn’t gave us the meaningful result. Anyways, I took control and eventually solved the problem. In 4 months I did all the experiments that the reviewers asked me to do. But the manuscript was resubmitted after 6 months of editing by my supervisor. However, at this instance reviewers were more positive about the manuscript but further suggested experiments and changes. I performed all the experiments and made sure that we resubmit the manuscript with changes within a month. After so much of hard work, it was finally accepted.

​Meanwhile, I got another motivation from my supervisor, she again reduced my fellowship. Reason – she doesn’t see me finishing Ph.D by the end of 4th year so in 5th year she has to entirely pay for my fellowship. So reducing my fellowship was her solution.

Although, it took 2 years to get the manuscript accepted for publishing but more importantly I learnt how to do research and publish. During the time I was repeating the experiments, I was also working on other proteins and generated the data to publish the second paper. For my second paper, I designed and planned experiments independently. And it was accepted with minor revision. Meanwhile, I started looking for post-doc positions and started applying with my CV and cover letter.

​I applied to all the people in the field I knew, most of them said they don’t have a funded position, some didn’t reply. In between all this, there was one PI who replied back to me and to my surprise she knew my work, but she too didn’t had a funded position. However, she was willing to support me if I want to apply for an independent fellowship. Eventually, I visited her lab in Germany and discussed ideas for post-doc application and it can’t be more dramatic or co-incidental. She was “the reviewer of my first paper”, about whom I said I’m learning more from the reviewer’s comments than from my supervisor. Finally, we ended up submitting for a fellowship application together and hope to work together in future.

​Overall, I worked a lot during my Ph.D. I optimized and established a number of new techniques and methods in the lab. Not only I published two first author papers. I also contributed to the two papers of my colleagues and generated data for another two papers which will be submitted soon.

​I had many downs in my Ph.D but at personal level, I always had the support of my father. Although, my dad is an engineer by profession and wouldn’t have understood any of my professional problems. But, he was always there to support me emotionally and financially. Without his sacrifices, understanding and support, I wouldn’t have achieved it.
